H&P – Super Detailed Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
40-year-old woman with childhood asthma presents with 2-day history of progressive wheeze and shortness of breath that began after heavy dust exposure while cleaning; no chest pain or dizziness; likely acute asthma flare vs. allergic dust reaction—GP evaluation with pulse-oximetry and possible medications advised.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Wheeze and shortness of breath.  
• Onset: ~1 hour after cleaning a dusty carpet 2 days ago.  
• Course/progression: Gradually worsening over 48 h; noticeably worse at night; today having difficulty completing sentences.  
• Aggravating factors: Night-time; talking; presumed dust exposure.  
• Relieving factors: None tried; has not used inhaler or taken medication.  
• Associated symptoms: Denies chest pain on deep inspiration; denies dizziness/vertigo. No cough, fever, nasal congestion, or rash mentioned.  
• Hydration/nutrition: Drinking 4–5 glasses of water/day; eating OK (details not elaborated).  
• Review of systems: No dizziness, no chest pain, no pleuritic pain; other systems not specifically queried.

Past Medical History:
• Childhood asthma – intermittent adult symptoms with prolonged running; possesses an old inhaler; prior courses of oral steroids (dates/doses not specified).  
• Seasonal allergic rhinitis (hay fever) in summer; untreated.  
• No known drug or environmental allergies reported.  
• No other chronic illnesses stated.

Medications:
• Salbutamol (presumed) inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented; not used for current episode.  
• No regular antihistamines or other medications.

Social History:
• No smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, occupation, or household details documented.  
• Recently exposed to large amount of dust while cleaning carpet.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
(No examination performed during video consultation; no vitals available.)

Investigations:
• None to date.  
• Planned: Office evaluation with pulse-oximetry; further lung function testing (“small device on finger” to check oxygen; possible additional tests per GP).

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Acute wheeze / probable asthma exacerbation triggered by dust  
– Childhood asthma history, typical nocturnal/worsening wheeze after allergen exposure.  
Plan:  
  • Same-day GP review for in-person assessment, pulse-oximetry, and objective lung function.  
  • Encourage use of available reliever inhaler en-route if breathlessness worsens (not explicitly stated in transcript but consistent with standard care; omit if strict).  
  • Consider short course of oral corticosteroids if objective evidence of airway obstruction (GP to decide).  
  • Provide GP letter via app documenting presentation.

Issue 2: Possible acute allergic reaction to dust-mite antigen  
Plan:  
  • Trial of oral, over-the-counter antihistamine (patient to purchase; cost ~£4–6) before/while attending GP visit.  
  • Monitor response; if significant improvement, continue antihistamine.

Issue 3: Rule-out other serious causes of acute dyspnoea (e.g., infection, PE)  
Plan:  
  • GP to perform full exam and consider further investigations (peak-flow, chest auscultation, CXR, D-dimer) if initial assessment atypical.

General advice:  
• Seek emergency care (999/ED) if severe breathlessness at rest, inability to speak, chest pain, or syncope.  
• Maintain hydration.  
• Follow-up after GP visit as advised.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Asthma exacerbation (High likelihood) – prior asthma, allergen trigger, nocturnal symptoms, expiratory wheeze pattern.  
2. Dust-induced allergic bronchospasm / allergic reaction (Moderate likelihood) – dust exposure, atopic history; lacks rapid resolution.  
3. Viral acute bronchitis (Low-moderate likelihood) – new respiratory symptoms without infection signs; less supported.  
Pulmonary embolism and other causes considered low but not excluded.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing but expected: Allergies confirmation, smoking/alcohol history, full medications list with doses, vital signs, objective peak-flow or O₂ saturation.  
• Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
• Transcript quality: Generally clear; one brief video drop but no critical data lost.
